Recommendation No.10 
Policy of ‘Care, Connect, Celebrate and Contribute’ 
 
The Committee observe that India’s Diaspora policy framework is centered around the 
four ‘C’s’ namely Care, Connect, Celebrate and Contribute. The Committee note that the 
shift in the Diaspora policy was brought about with the merger of the Ministry of Overseas 
Indian Affairs and the Ministry of External Affairs in January 2016. While acknowledging 
that the 4Cs uphold the welfare and protection of our Diaspora, connect them to their 
roots, and celebrate their achievements, the Committee feel that India’s Diaspora policy is 
still at nascent stage. Much needs to be done to tap into the potential of Indians living 
abroad and policy document on its Diaspora needs to be drafted by the Government. The 
Committee do not agree with the Ministry’s perception that the diversity of Indian 
Diaspora does not permit formulation of a single, tight and unique policy. The Committee 
are of the considered view that lack of a dedicated Diaspora policy document hinders our 
ability to fully leverage the potential of the large overseas Indian community, impacting 
economic growth, foreign relations, knowledge transfer, and overall national development 
by limiting engagement with skilled professionals and investors living abroad, while also 
failing to adequately address the concerns and needs of the Diaspora population. The 
Committee, therefore, desire that the Ministry bring out a policy document on Indian 
Diaspora in tune with their aspirations to serve as a guiding principle for deeper and wider 
engagement with the Diaspora community. 
Reply of the Government 
The Government of India’s approach to engaging with the Indian Diaspora is focussed on the 
four foundational pillars: Care, Connect, Celebrate, and Contribute. These four ‘C’s form the 
core of a pragmatic, inclusive and dynamic Diaspora Engagement Policy, designed to protect the 
interests of Indians abroad while maximizing the mutual benefits of this global community’s 
links with India. Since the merger of the Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs (MOIA) with the 
Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) in 2016, this integrated approach has led to more coherent, 
responsive, and effective outreach, which can be outlined as follows. 
 
(I) Care for the Indian communities overseas: Safeguarding the Welfare of Our Diaspora 

Page | 87 
 
 
The “Care” pillar reflects the government’s commitment to the protection and welfare of Indian 
citizens and persons of Indian origin abroad, especially the vulnerable and distressed. 
 
Key schemes and mechanisms of the Government to promote the Pillar: 
 
i. Indian Community Welfare Fund (ICWF) – Emergency support for distressed overseas 
Indians, including repatriation, shelter medical aid, legal assistance, and transfer of 
mortal remains. 
 
ii. One Stop Centers (OSC) – Centers in select Indian Embassies and Consulates to provide 
emergency shelter, police help, and medical and legal assistance to women in distress.  
 
iii. e-Migrate System – Ensures safe and transparent emigration processes, especially for 
ECR passport holders. 
 
iv. Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana (PBBY) – A welfare scheme providing insurance 
coverage to Indian workers abroad to ensure their safety and support in cases of 
emergencies. 
 
v. MADAD Portal – Online platform for consular grievance redressal in a time bound 
manner. 
 
vi. Pre-Departure Orientation Programme (P-DOT) - One-day training programme on soft 
skills for migrant workers imparted by MEA in collaboration with National Skill 
Development Corporation (NSDC), State Governments and other stake holders. 
 
vii. Scholarship Programme for Diaspora Children (SPDC) – Financial assistance for the 
children of Persons of Indian Origin (PIOs) and Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) for 
pursuing undergraduate education at Indian universities and institutions. 
 
viii. Migration and Mobility Agreements – Partnership agreements with key countries to 
harness India’s demographic dividend and foster mobility for Indian students, academics, 
business people, and professionals.  
 

Page | 88 
 
ix. Assistance in Marital & Child Custody Matters – Support for Indian women facing 
abandonment or abuse abroad. 
 
x. Support in NRI Property Disputes and Student Grievances – Coordination with law 
enforcement and educational institutions. 
 
 
(II) Connect with the global network of Indian diaspora: Bridging Indians Worldwide with 
Their Roots 
 
Under “Connect”, the focus is on forging deeper links between India and its global communities 
through institutional networks and cultural ties.  
 
Key schemes and mechanisms of the Government to promote this Pillar: 
 
i. Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD) - A flagship event that provides a platform for 
engagement between the Government and the Diaspora. 
 
ii. Know India Programme (KIP) – Designed for diaspora youth to explore India’s history, 
heritage, and governance through first hand experience 
 
iii. Global Pravasi Rishta Portal – A two-way digital portal to connect the Indian Diaspora 
with the Government of India for dissemination of important information and to foster a 
robust database of the Diaspora through voluntary registrations. 
 
iv. Promotion of Cultural Ties with Diaspora (PCTD) – Grants extended to Indian 
Embassies/Consulates for organizing cultural events abroad for promoting heritage and 
for encouraging the diaspora to stay connected to their cultural roots. 
 
v. Videsh Sampark Programme – Outreach to State governments to address the challenges 
faced by the Indian States to deal with diaspora related issues and to suggest efforts to 
promote robust dialogue between the Indian States and their respective Diaspora. 
 

Page | 89 
 
vi. Pravasi Teerth Darshan Yojna (PTDY) – Offers an opportunity for the Indian diaspora to 
visit places of religious and cultural significance in India. 
 
vii. Bharat Ko Janiye (BKJ) Quiz – Quiz contest for diaspora youth to deepen their 
knowledge of India and organisation of exposure trips for the winners to India. 
 
viii. Social Media Outreach – Daily engagement campaigns like Diaspora India Connect on 
social media platforms 
 
(III) Celebrate India’s shared heritage with the wide network of global Indian diaspora: 
Honoring Shared Culture and Achievements of the Diaspora 
 
“Celebrate” emphasizes the acknowledgement of India’s rich heritage and the remarkable 
contributions of overseas Indians not only to their host countries, but also to the Indian 
community, society and economy. 
 
Key schemes and mechanisms of the Government directed towards promoting this Pillar: 
 
i. Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD) – Biennial Convention with special sessions to recognize 
and discuss the contributions of the Indian diaspora in diverse domains. 
 
ii. Pravasi Bharatiya Samman Awards (PBSA) – India’s highest honor for overseas Indians, 
awarded for their outstanding achievements in myriad fields. 
 
iii. Girmitiya Engagement – Research, outreach, and future establishment of Girmitiya Study 
and Research Center to connect with descendants of indentured Indians and celebrate 
their legacy. 
 
(IV) Encourage Contributions of the Indian diaspora that drive positive change in India: 
Tapping Diaspora Potential for National Development 
 
The “Contribute” pillar encourages the diaspora to participate in India's developmental journey 
by sharing their knowledge, skills, etc and through investments, and innovation. 

Page | 90 
 
 
Key schemes and mechanisms of the Government to promote this Pillar: 
 
i. Knowledge sharing initiatives such as VAJRA (Visiting Advanced Joint Research 
Faculty Scheme), PRABHASS (Pravasi Bharatiya Academic and Scientific Sampark) and 
Vaishvik Bharatiya Vaigyanik (VAIBHAV) fellowships, to promote collaborations 
between global Indian scientists and researchers with Indian institutions. 
 
ii. Promotion of Start-up India, Digital India, and other key programmes that welcome 
diaspora-led innovations and investments. 
 
iii. Ministry also works closely with the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Commerce, RBI, 
and other relevant institutions to ensure seamless remittance channels for Indian diaspora, 
promotes Unified Payments Interface (UPI) linkages, disseminates updated information 
regarding tax laws, FEMA provisions, Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements, FDI 
norms, etc. 
 
While this Ministry has a reasonably well-defined Diaspora Engagement Policy based on the 
aforesaid enumerated 4Cs and has devised effective strategies/schemes to promote the same, still 
it is the considered view and experience of this Ministry that the vast diversity of the Indian 
diaspora demands flexibility. So, although this Ministry takes note of the Committee’s 
recommendation to create a tighter, codified Diaspora Policy, it woulde prefer to maintain that a 
“single, tight and unique policy document” on Indian diaspora may not be conducive to serve the 
growing and dynamic aspirations of the Indian diaspora spread across the globe because of the 
inherent diversity and complexity of the diaspora itself. Their needs, expectations, legal status, 
socio-economic contexts vary dramatically across regions, from the Silicon Valley to the Gulf 
region or the Girmitiya countries. A central and rigid policy could also undermine or overlook 
state-level priorities, which are often more attuned to specific community needs. A dedicated 
Diaspora policy should also align with the laws of the host country, which differ across regions, 
and may have specific elements such as dual citizenship restrictions, data privacy laws, labour 
rights, etc.  
 
The 4C-based Diaspora Policy of the Government functions as a comprehensive and dynamic 
mechanism to engage with the large and diverse Indian diaspora that encompasses addressing 
their welfare, cultural preservation, economic collaboration, and institutional dialogue. Going 
forward, efforts can focus on strengthening coordination, enhancing digital access, and 

Page | 91 
 
expanding the scope of existing schemes, so that the 4Cs continue to be the most effective and 
inclusive pathway to fostering a vibrant, connected, and empowered Indian diaspora across the 
globe.

Recommendation No.37

The Committee note that as per the information available with the Ministry, about 5,95,101

stricter immigration policies and a reduction in job opportunities abroad has created 
considerable reintegration challenges. The Committee note that a national level policy on 
re-integration of migrant returnees is still awaited. The Committee further note that 
Kerala is the only State in India that offers economic reintegration and welfare 
programmes for returning migrants, all of which are worth emulating by other States and 
even other countries.  The Committee are of the view that though the responsibility for 
rehabilitation of Indian migrants is currently placed on State Governments, with the 
Central Government providing neither logistical nor financial support, it is high time that

responsibilities between the Centre and State Governments. The Committee, therefore,

that responsibility of reintegration of returned Indian migrants rests with respective State 
Governments from where the emigrants belong and not with the Central Government. Various

Recommendation No.4 
Aadhaar Facilitation for Overseas Indians 
 
The Committee note that Overseas Indians are facing difficulties in getting Aadhaar 
Cards in the country. The Committee have been given to understand that UIDAI, which 
is the competent authority in the matter has not made any arrangement for setting up 
Aadhaar facilitation centers outside India. Today, in India, Aadhaar is an essential 
document providing a portable proof of identity verifiable through Aadhaar 
authentication on-line anytime, anywhere. An Aadhaar Card is an essential document for 
literally every form of registration and transaction facilitating access to various services 
like banking, property transactions, healthcare and government benefits, especially when 
the card holders reside in the country for extended periods, while also streamlining 
processes like tax filing and KYC verification. The Committee are of the considered view 
that extending facility of Aadhaar cards to Overseas Indians will promote greater 
integration of Indians living abroad into the Indian society. The extension of the facility 
of Aadhaar cards to Overseas Indians will also align with the goal of creating a unified 
identity system in India, enabling them to participate fully in the country's economic and 
social activities while maintaining their non-resident status. The Committee, therefore, 
urge the Ministry to work in coordination with UIDAI in identifying the bottlenecks 
involved, including procedural difficulties, technical grievances etc., and resolve the 
same. 
 
Reply of the Government 
The Ministry agrees with the Committee’s recommendation that extension of the facility of 
Aadhaar cards to Overseas Indians may contribute towards integrating the Indian diaspora 
more comprehensively into the Indian economy and society. However, the proposal entails 
significant complexities and challenges that are outlined here. 
 
 Aadhaar is governed by the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other 
Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016, which explicitly defines eligibility based on 
residency in India. The Act defines a "resident" as an individual who has been in India for a 
cumulative period of 182 days or more within the 12 months preceding their application for 
Aadhaar enrolment. This residency requirement applies to all individuals, including Non-
Resident Indians (NRIs), who wish to obtain an Aadhaar card. Extending Aadhaar to non-

Page | 104 
 
residents would require fundamental amendments to the Act. Moreover, establishing biometric 
enrolment infrastructure in foreign countries would be logistically complex, costly, and could 
conflict with data protection laws in host countries such as the European Union’s GDPR and 
similar frameworks elsewhere. This exposes the Indian government to litigation risks, 
diplomatic tensions, or data localization demands by host nations. Additionally, collecting 
sensitive biometric data abroad introduces the risk of identity duplication and verification 
difficulties, potentially compromising the reliability of the Aadhaar ecosystem. 
 
 For the diaspora members who do not reside in India, or do financial transactions in 
India or require access to Indian subsidies or government services, the practical benefits of 
Aadhaar are limited. Existing identity mechanisms such as passports, OCI/PIO cards, 
NRE/NRO bank accounts and PAN numbers already serve many of their financial and legal 
needs in India. The diaspora members who stand to benefit the most with Aadhaar are also 
likely to travel frequently to India, during which they can obtain their cards through the 
widespread and robust network of Aadhaar centers in the country. 
 
 The Ministry remains committed to facilitating and enhancing the engagement of the 
Indian diaspora with India. In pursuance of the Committee’s recommendation, Ministry has 
written to UIDAI to explore the feasibility of extending Aadhaar universally. The comments 
from UIDAI are awaited.

Recommendation No.41 
Creation of a Centralised, Real-Time Migration Database 
 
Effective policymaking requires robust migration data governance. While acknowledging 
that MEA’s PoE offices track Emigration Clearance Required (ECR) data, and migration 
estimates exist from Census 2011 and the National Sample Survey 2020-21, the Committee 
note that a centralised, real-time migration database remains absent. They, therefore, 
recommend that under the proposed new legislation, the Government must make provision 
for establishing a national migration database or social registry, to track outgoing and 
returnee migrants, their skills, employment sectors, and remittance patterns. Integrating 
passport, visa and emigration data portals would positively aid policy formulation and 
social welfare provisioning. 
Reply of the Government 
This Ministry agrees with the Committee’s observation that strengthening migration data 
governance is a critical component of effective policymaking that will positively aid policy 

Page | 114 
 
formulation and social welfare provisioning. The Government has already laid strong 
foundational work through interlinked digital platforms and ongoing integration efforts. It has 
instituted and constantly enhances key systems such as the eMigrate portal, which manages 
emigration clearance, labour contracts, and welfare registration for ECR passport holders; 
Passport Seva system, which is a digitized and globally accessible passport issuance platform; 
MADAD portal, which facilitates grievance redressal and enables real-time feedback; Global 
Pravasi Rishta portal, which aims to create a voluntary database of Indian diaspora, etc. 
 
However, the creation of a centralised real-time migration database at a global scale presents 
major challenges. Migration of Indians has a dynamic and decentralised nature. They move 
across countries for a wide range of purposes and through formal and informal channels. Many 
diaspora members are long-settled citizens or permanent residents of host countries and are not 
consistently captured in any existing Indian database. Tracking them in real time across 
jurisdictions to create a database could discourage voluntary registrations by migrants, especially 
those in irregular or transitional employment.  
 
Moreover, collecting, storing, and transmitting personal data of migrants abroad raises serious 
concerns under host country privacy laws. Without express consent or bilateral data-sharing 
agreements, maintaining a live registry could lead to diplomatic sensitivities and violate local 
data protection norms. 
 
Therefore, a balanced and targeted approach is preferred by enhancing the existing systems of 
data capture and promoting interoperability between them, in collaboration with other concerned 
Ministries. This Ministry has initiated discussions with the Bureau of Immigration to explore the 
feasibility of an integrated migration data system, in order to build a robust, data-driven, people-
centric migration governance framework. Their comments/inputs are awaited.

Report on the 18th Pravasi Bharatiya Divas Convention 2025 
 
Background: 
  
 Government of India launched its flagship Pravasi Bharatiya Divas Convention in the year 2003 
with a view to strengthen its engagement with the overseas Indian community. It was part of its endeavor 
to celebrate the remarkable achievements of the esteemed Indian community living across the globe and 
to recognise their contributions to the development of India besides reconnecting them with their cultural 
roots. January 09 was chosen as a day to celebrate the occasion since it was on this day in the year 1915 
that Mahatma Gandhi, the most influential Pravasi, returned to India from South Africa, to lead India’s 
freedom struggle that changed the lives of Indians forever.

being celebrated on a biennial basis in partnership with a State Government of India. Indian Diaspora 
Members are encouraged to participate in the event to explore the rich cultural heritage of India. The 
Convention provides a platform to leverage the expertise of the Indian Diaspora in technology, education, 
innovation, attract investments and entrepreneurship, and promote India’s global soft power. These 
Conventions also provide an avenue for the overseas Indian community to engage with the Government 
and the people of the land of their ancestors for undertaking mutually beneficial activities. These 
Conventions have proved to be very useful for facilitating networking amongst the overseas Indian 
community residing in various parts of the world and to enable them to share their expertise in various 
fields. Till the year 2023, 17 editions of the Pravasi Bharatiya Divas Convention were held, the last being

I am very pleased to welcome you all to the Youth Pravasi Bharatiya Divas 2025

younger generation as part of the PBD celebrations. The thinking behind that is 
one of recognizing the special contribution that young minds make, at home and 
abroad. And indeed, in connecting them more effectively for mutual good. At a 
time when so many key developments in the world are being shaped by this 
younger generation – whether we talk of AI and EV, innovation or startups, space

was predicted to go under ended up supplying vaccines and medicines to the 
entire world. A different but equally telling example is what we see in the realm of 
space, where there is a growing competition internationally. Our Chandrayaan-3

Ladies and Gentlemen, 
I take this opportunity to extend congratulate Her Excellency Christine Kangaloo, 
President of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago, on being conferred with the 
Pravasi Bharatiya Samman 2025. Excellency, your outstanding contributions in 
leading your nation, with a special focus on women and the Indian diaspora, has set 
a high benchmark on the world stage. This is a reflection of the deep ties of 
friendship and cooperation between our two countries, as much as it is a testament 
of the shared values that bind us across borders. 
Ladies and Gentlemen, 
The Indian Diaspora represents the best of our country. You, the sons and daughters 
of Bharat, have carried with you not just the knowledge and skills acquired in this 
sacred land, but also the values and ethos that have been the foundation of our 
civilization for millennia. Whether in the fields of technology, medicine, arts, or 
entrepreneurship, the Indian Diaspora has made a mark that the world 
acknowledges and respects. 
Today, we honour those amongst you who have distinguished themselves through 
exemplary achievements. It is my privilege to confer on them the Pravasi Bharatiya 
Samman, as India’s token of recognition of their extraordinary contributions. My 
heartfelt congratulations to all the awardees. Your success stories are not just a 
matter of pride for India, but they also inspire millions across the world to strive for 
excellence. 
Ladies and Gentlemen, 
The Pravasi Bharatiya Divas has, over the years, become more than just an event; it 
is a platform where ideas converge, collaborations are forged, and the bonds 

Page | 159 
 
between India and its Diaspora are strengthened. I am sure that over the last three 
days, you have used this occasion to engage in meaningful dialogue, and share 
your experiences. This event underscores the fact that while you may be physically 
distant from your homeland, your connections with Bharat remain as strong as ever. 
 
Ladies and Gentlemen, 
Our nation today is marching towards Viksit Bharat – a developed India – by the 
year 2047, when we will celebrate 100 years of our independence. This vision is not 
just a government initiative; it is a National Mission that requires proactive and 
enthusiastic participation of every Indian, including those living abroad. 
The Indian Diaspora is an integral part of this vision. Your global presence gives you 
a unique perspective, and your achievements place you in a position to significantly 
contribute to the realization of a developed India. I have seen this first-hand during 
my interactions with our Diaspora as part of my travels abroad. I urge you all to 
actively engage in this journey, for in your success, lies the success of India. 
Ladies and Gentlemen, 
Recognising the crucial role of the Diaspora in nation-building, Government of India 
has undertaken several initiatives to support you. Consular services for Non 
Resident Indians (NRIs) have been simplified. For Overseas Citizens of India 
(OCIs), processes have been digitized and streamlined. Initiatives like “Know India 
Programme” provide avenues for the younger members of our Diaspora to re-
discover their Indian roots. 
I am happy to know that Odisha Government is appointing a Nodal Minister for 
engaging with Pravasi Bharatiya for projects, investments, etc. I appreciate the step 
taken by the Odisha Government. 
We have also been proactive in safeguarding interests of Indians living abroad. In 
recent years, we have launched several missions, including Operation Kaveri, 
Operation Ganga and Operation Vande Bharat, to assist distressed Indians. Today, 
Indians around the world can count on their homeland for support and protection in 
times of need. 
Ladies and Gentlemen, 
Over the last three days, experts from diverse fields have come together here to 
discuss issues of importance, for both India as well its Diaspora. You all must have 
seen the special exhibits at the Convention, which highlight various important facets 
of our Diaspora’s connection and contributions to India. I am sure these insightful 
discussions will help to shape policies that benefit both India and the global 
community. 

Page | 160 
 
A special mention must also be made of the contributions of women, students, and 
the youth amongst our Diaspora. The achievements of Indian women globally are a 
matter of immense pride for us, as they break barriers and scale new heights in 
various fields. Our students and youth, with their dynamism and creativity, are the 
torchbearers of our future. They are the ones who will carry forward the legacy of a 
vibrant and progressive India. 
Ladies and Gentlemen, 
Our vision for Viksit Bharat aligns with our growing stature on the world stage, 
particularly as a leading voice for the Global South. It is guided by our timeless 
philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, or 'The World is One Family’. 
This vision is about creating an ecosystem that not only meets our needs, but also 
contributes to global well-being. We seek to be a nation that balances economic 
progress with social justice and environmental stewardship, ensuring a bright future 
for generations to come. Each one of you, whether through entrepreneurship, 
philanthropy, or knowledge-sharing, will play an essential role in achieving this 
vision. 
Ladies and Gentlemen, 
The connection between the Indian Diaspora and the Motherland is eternal. No 
matter where you are in the world, Bharat is and will always be your home. This 
bond is rooted in shared heritage, culture, and values. It is this connection that we 
celebrate today, and it is this connection that will continue to inspire us as we move 
forward together. 
As we celebrate the achievements of our Pravasi Bharatiya family, let us also look 
forward to the future with hope and determination. Together, we can build a Viksit 
Bharat, a nation that stands tall on the global stage and continues to be a beacon of 
light for the world. 
Thank you, 
Jai Hind! 
Jai Bharat!

CHAPTER 1 
ANALYSIS OF DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2026-27) 
 The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) formulates and conducts India’s foreign 
policy within the framework of our values and principles of fostering international 
peace and cooperation with the overall objective of meeting India’s strategic aims 
and aspirations as well as to secure our national interests. In pursuance of its 
mandated objectives, the MEA headquarters in New Delhi is assisted by 231 
Missions and Posts abroad, its Branch Secretariats and 37 Passport Offices in India, 
and autonomous bodies funded by it. The Ministry is also supported by other 
Ministries and State Governments which also contribute to India’s international 
engagement in consultation and coordination with MEA. 
1.2 Under the Constitution of India [Article 113 (2)], estimates of expenditure is 
submitted to Lok Sabha in the form of Demands for Grants. The Demands for Grants 
of the Ministry of External Affairs (Demand No. 29) was laid on the table of the House 
on 12 February 2026.

14748.99 crore (71.89% of BE 2025-26 & 67.83 % of RE 2025-26). The allocation in

their host nations while maintaining deep and enduring ties with the motherland.

within the MEA handles matters relating to Diaspora, their welfare and emigration”

relating to students and NRI marital disputes issues along with 
programmes related with engagement of Diaspora which includes Know 
India Programme (KIP), Scholarship Programme for Diaspora Children 
(SPDC), Promotion of Cultural Ties with Diaspora (PCTD), celebration of 
Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD) etc.

matters relating to Migration and Mobility including MMPAs & LMAs, 
Emigration Bill, India-EU CAMM, Global Compact on Migration, ADD, 
IMRF and other Regional Processes along with welfare initiatives for 
Indian workers abroad like PDOT, PBBY, ICWF & PKVY.

Division: This Division deals with matters related to overseas employment 
of Indian workers, appointment of overseas recruitment agents, providing 
assistance through Pravasi Bharatiya  Sahatya Kendra (PBSK), working of 
E-Migrate Portal, Welfare measures to protect the interests of Emigrants 
working abroad etc.

Ministry provides passport services through the Central Passport 
Organization (CPO) and its network of Passport Offices, Passport Seva

III. EMIGRATION 
2.35 In recent times, international migration has assumed a pivotal role, shaped by 
demographic shifts and technological progress, significantly impacting labour 
markets worldwide. India is a leading country in the international migration dynamics 
and is advantageously poised due to its demographic potential. The emigration of 
Indian workers, particularly low-skilled and semi-skilled workers proceeding to the 
nineteen notified Emigration Check Required (ECR) countries of the Gulf, South-East 
Asia, and beyond, represents one of the most consequential and most vulnerable 
dimensions of India’s external engagement. The primary legal framework governing 
their emigration is the Emigration Act, 1983. 
Protector of Emigrants 
2.36 With the help of 16 offices of the Protector of Emigrants (POEs) located at 
Mumbai, Chennai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chandigarh, Hyderabad, Kochi, 
Thiruvananthapuram, Jaipur, Lucknow, Patna, Bengaluru, Guwahati, Ranchi, 
Bhubaneswar and Agartala, the Protector General of Emigrants (PGE) enforces the 
Emigration Act, 1983. The Protectors of Emigrants performs functions assigned to 
them by this Act under the general superintendence and control of the Protector 
General of Emigrants. The main function of the Protector of Emigrants includes the 
grant of Emigration Clearance to the emigrants to ECR (Emigration Check Required) 
Countries as per the procedure prescribed under the Emigration Act, 1983, 
monitoring of recruitment process and reporting illegal agents, inspection of office 
premises of prospective Recruiting Agents (RAs) as they apply for the Registration 
Certificate and helping the Protector General of Emigrants in implementation of 
Emigration Act, 1983. As per the Act, the Recruiting Agents (RAs) are required to 
obtain Registration Certificate (RC) from the PGE before they could engage in 
recruitment for overseas employment. Emigration of ECR passport holders is 
regulated by way of grant of Emigration Clearance (EC) by any of the above 16 
officers of the POEs for employment in any of the 19 notified ECR countries, namely, 
Afghanistan, Bahrain, Indonesia, Iraq, Iran, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, 

39 | P a g e 
 
Malaysia, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria, Thailand, United 
Arab Emirates and Yemen. 
2.37 The mandate and core responsibilities of the Protector of Emigrants are 
defined under the Emigration Act, 1983. These duties of PoEs have been elaborated 
under Section 4 of the ibid act, as "General duties of Protectors of Emigrants—
Subject to the other provisions of this Act, every Protector of Emigrants shall, in 
addition to the special duties assigned to him by or under this Act —  
(a) protect and aid with his advice all intending emigrants and emigrants;  
(b) cause, so far as he can, all the provisions of this Act and of the rules made 
thereunder to be complied with;  
(c) inspect, to such extent and in such manner as may be prescribed— 
(i) any emigrant conveyance, or 
(ii) any other conveyance if he has reason to believe that any intending 
emigrants or emigrants are proceeding from, or returning to, India to or from a 
place outside India by such other conveyance; 
(d) aid and advise, so far as he reasonably can, emigrants who have returned to 
India. 
2.38 Apart from above duties following responsibilities have been entrusted to the 
Protector of Emigrants: 
a. Emigration Clearance: Granting Emigration Clearance (EC) to individuals 
intending to go abroad for employment to notified ECR countries, ensuring that 
applications are thoroughly verified and meet all legal requirements. 
b. Guidance and Protection: Providing comprehensive protection and guidance to 
prospective emigrants and those already deployed abroad. This includes 
rendering timely and effective advice and assistance throughout their journey and 
employment abroad. 
c. Regulatory Compliance: Ensuring all stakeholders, including Recruiting Agents 
(RAs), comply with the Emigration Act, 1983, and relevant regulations, thereby 
maintaining the integrity of the emigration system. 

40 | P a g e 
 
d. Grievance Redressal: Addressing grievances from emigrants regarding 
repatriation, employment disputes, and related issues, ensuring quick resolution 
and support. 
e. Coordination with Authorities: Engaging with the Bureau of Immigration, State 
Police, Indian Embassies, and Consulates, as well as other relevant government 
agencies, to protect emigrant welfare and enforce compliance. 
f. Monitoring and Investigation: Conducting thorough investigations into the 
treatment of emigrants, both during transit and their stay abroad, and taking 
corrective actions if required. 
g. Educational and Outreach Programs: Organizing educational initiatives and 
outreach programs to inform and educate emigrants and stakeholders about safe 
and legal migration practices. Pre-departure Orientation Training for emigrants is 
an important initiative in this direction.  
h. Policy Implementation and Feedback: Implementing policy changes and 
providing feedback to the PGE Division and Ministry of External Affairs to 
continuously enhance emigration processes and safeguard emigrant interests.

2.44 Elaborating the emigration clearance process work in PoE offices, the Ministry 
stated that since 2014, the Ministry of External Affairs has started granting of online 
Emigration Clearance (EC) to the Indian Emigrants through the eMigrate portal 
(www.emigrate.gov.in)  only. The detailed process for grant of EC is as follows: 

43 | P a g e 
 
a. Demand initiation: The Foreign Employer (FE) raises a demand, providing 
essential details such as vacancies, job roles, and employment conditions. 
The RA acknowledges the demand, verifying authenticity and compliance of 
the documents, including the labor quota and contract documentation. 
b. Application submission: The emigrant or the recruiting agent (RA) submits 
an online application through the eMigrate portal after paying relevant fees 
and uploading necessary documents like the passport, visa, employment 
contract, and insurance policy. Document requirements may vary from country 
to country. 
c. Verification by CPC and Passport validation: Passport validation occurs by 
cross-checking with the Passport database of the Ministry of External Affairs 
(MEA). The Central Processing Center (CPC) conducts detailed verification of 
submitted documents, employment contracts, insurance coverage, and 
compliance with prescribed rates and emigration regulations. 
d. File forward and review: Verified files are forwarded by the CPC with 
comments to the concerned Protector of Emigrants (PoE), who reviews the 
documents and either approves or rejects the emigration clearance, providing 
clear justifications in case of rejections. 
e. Update of records: The eMigrate system is updated with the clearance 
status to reflect the outcome of the application process. 
f. Sharing of data and verification of EC at airport: Clearance data is integrated 
and shared with Bureau of Immigration (BOI) check posts to ensure seamless 
processing and monitoring of emigrant travel. At the airport, immigration 
officials verify aspects like Emigration Clearance status, Visa details etc. Exit 
from India is allowed only if the emigrant intending to travel abroad to notified 
ECR countries for employment purposes, has valid clearance. 
2.45 The Committee further enquired about safeguards are in place within PoE

recruitment agencies or unauthorized intermediaries. In a written reply the Ministry

clearance process is not misused or circumvented by illegal recruitment agencies or 
unauthorized intermediaries.  
a. Digital verification: All the Emigration Clearances (ECs) are applied and 
processed through the eMigrate portal only, ensuring that only authorized agents 
registered with the Ministry can apply for EC. The Bureau of Immigration (BOI) will

c. Strict recruiting agent (RA) registration: A rigorous vetting process (compulsory 
police and degree verification) is in place for registering and renewing Recruiting 
Agent licenses. 
d. Initiating actions: Show cause notices are issued to registered RAs involved in 
illegal activities. Those violating provisions of the Emigration Act 1983 are 
suspended as necessary. Additionally, action is taken against illegal/unregistered 
RAs in coordination with local police under various provisions of the Emigration 
Act. 
e. Surprise inspections: Unannounced checks on RAs deter illegal activities and 
ensure compliance. 
f. Coordination with law enforcement: Working closely with police and cyber crime

violations with each other.

3.11  To a query of the Committee regarding the challenges faced by the Ministry in 
implementation of development partnership in other countries, the Ministry in a written reply 
has stated that implementation of large infrastructure projects is a challenging task 
irrespective of their location. The challenges are further increased when such projects are 
undertaken abroad. The nature of challenges varies from country to country depending upon 
the special circumstances under which the project is to operate. Some common issues faced 
during project execution or implementation include non-availability of encumbrance-free site, 
difficulties in land acquisition, Right of Way issues, contractual issues, delays in 
environmental impact assessments, etc. Apart from these, other major challenges include 
the changing politico-security situation in countries abroad which renders changed priority 
accorded to the project. It has been India’s endeavour to put in place a robust mechanism for 
handling all aspects of project implementation, including project formulation, appraisal, 
execution, monitoring, review and evaluation, so that challenges facing projects are 
approached in a systematic and organized manner. Priority is given to the efforts to closely 
involve and engage the host beneficiary government and other stakeholders in all aspects of 
the project to manage the challenges in nascent stage and alleviate their impact.

CHAPTER 4 
ISSUANCE OF PASSPORT 
Passport services constitute one of the most visible and citizen-centric 
functions discharged by the Ministry of External Affairs. A passport, as a document of 
national identity and sovereign guarantee, is issued under the authority of the 
Passports Act, 1967, and represents the State's formal undertaking to afford 
protection to its bearer in foreign jurisdictions. The Government of India, recognizing 
the growing demand for passport services driven by increasing outward mobility, a 
large and expanding diaspora, and rising aspirations of its citizens, has over the 
years undertaken a series of structural, technological, and administrative reforms to 
make passport issuance more accessible, transparent, and efficient. The 
establishment of the Passport Seva Programme under a Public-Private Partnership 
model marked a watershed in the delivery of passport services, transforming what 
was once a largely manual and time-consuming process into a technology-driven, 
citizen-friendly system operational across an extensive network of Passport Seva 
Kendras and Post Office Passport Seva Kendras spread throughout the country.

5.52 The Committee wanted to know about the key principles shaping and guiding 
Indian foreign policy making in the changed international order. In a written response 
the Ministry stated that the world is transitioning into a more multipolar world. There 
has been a change in the nature and distribution of power. The contemporary 
geopolitical and geoeconomic realities do not reflect conventional bipolar or unipolar 
models.  Consequently, many more countries are in a position to influence and shape 
outcomes. In this increasing multipolarity, India aspires to occupy one of the key 
poles of the emerging geopolitical landscape. This can be achieved by optimal 
combination of capabilities, relationships and positioning. India’s ability to move 
forward in this loose architecture of multiple interest-based alliances will determine 
the path towards it emerging as a leading power in coming times. 
5.53 Given the rapidly changing international scenario and the evolving international 
order, India continues to pursue its pragmatic and outcome oriented engagements to 

117 | P a g e 
 
enhance security, upholding its territorial integrity and promote economic 
transformation. India pursues these goals through strengthened bilateral, regional 
and multilateral partnerships. While India strives to build its influence in key global 
forums, it is also offering to the world its own unique solutions to global issues, like 
the International Solar Alliance (ISA) and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient 
Infrastructure (CDRI).  Our neighbourhood and the Indian Ocean Region will continue 
to be accorded the highest priority, where the focus will be on creating mutually 
beneficial people oriented regional frameworks for stability and prosperity.

India maintains an extensive network of Missions and Posts abroad, 
comprising Embassies, High Commissions, Consulates General, Consulates, and 
other diplomatic offices, which together constitute the primary institutional 
mechanism through which the Government of India pursues its foreign policy 
objectives and manages its external engagements. Established under the provisions 
of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961, and the Vienna Convention 
on Consular Relations, 1963, these Missions and Posts are mandated to represent 
India's sovereign interests, strengthen bilateral and multilateral relations, promote 
trade, investment, and cultural ties, and provide consular and passport services to 
Indian nationals residing or travelling abroad. As on date, the Ministry of External 
Affairs administers a total of 219 Missions and Posts making India's diplomatic 
network one of the most expansive among developing nations.

Overall Budgetary Allocation for 2026-27 
1. The Committee note that the Ministry of External Affairs has been 
allocated Rs. 22,118.97 crore in Budget Estimates (BE) 2026-27. This 
represents an increase of 7.81% over BE 2025-26 of Rs. 20,516.61 crore and 
1.73% over Revised Estimates (RE) 2025-26 of Rs. 21,742.74 crore. As a 
proportion of the total Union Budget 2026-27, the MEA's allocation stands at 
0.41%, which is the same as in 2025-26. The Committee observe that while the 
absolute allocation has increased in nominal terms, the proportional share has 
remained relatively low, even as India's global ambitions, diplomatic footprint, 
and development partnership commitments have expanded substantially. 
The Committee are concerned to note that the budgetary allocation for 
the Ministry of External Affairs as a percentage of the total Union Budget has 
declined consistently from 0.69% in 2017-18 to 0.41% in 2026-27. In absolute 
terms, India allocates approximately 0.06% of its GDP to foreign affairs, which 
compares unfavourably with countries such as the United States 
(approximately 0.15-0.20% of GDP) and United Kingdom (approximately 0.25-
0.30% of GDP). The Committee further note that MEA is ranked 23rd among 
Union Ministries in terms of budgetary allocation at Rs. 22,118.97 crore in BE 
2026-27, despite being entrusted with managing India's entire external 
engagement at a time when India occupies an increasingly prominent position 
in global affairs. 
In its Fifth Report on DFG 2025-26, the Committee had specifically 
recommended a budgetary enhancement of at least 20% in allocation to MEA. 
The Ministry has conveyed that this recommendation was formally 
communicated to the Ministry of Finance by the Foreign Secretary ahead of the 
pre-budget consultations. Despite this, the eventual increase has been limited 
to 7.81% - well short of what the Committee had recommended. The Committee 
are constrained to observe that this level of increase is inadequate to keep 
pace with India's expanding international engagements and the rising costs of 

187 | P a g e 
 
diplomacy. The Committee therefore, strongly recommend that due cognizance 
should to be given to the strategic imperatives driving MEA's expenditure and 
accord the Ministry a budgetary allocation commensurate with India's 
aspirations as a leading global power. The Committee reiterate their earlier 
recommendation for a budgetary enhancement of at least 20% and urge that 
the MEA's allocation be progressively raised to a level closer to the global 
benchmark for comparable major economies. The concern of the Committee 
may be conveyed to the Ministry of the Finance for further necessary action.

2. The Committee note that MEA currently ranks 23rd among all Ministries 
and Departments in terms of budgetary allocation, at 0.41% of the Union 
Budget. Ministries such as Finance (35.93%), Defence (14.29%), Road 
Transport and Highways (5.64%), and Railways (5.12%) understandably 
command larger shares given their domestic infrastructure mandates. 
However, the Committee are of the view that MEA's allocation must be 
compared not merely in terms of rank but in terms of the strategic multiplier it 
provides: effective diplomatic engagement secures trade, investment, 
Diaspora welfare, neighbourhood stability, and India's standing in multilateral 
institutions - dividends that accrue across sectors and are not fully captured in 
any single Ministry's budget. 
The Committee had persistently recommended that the Ministry should

in a comparative framework. Pursuant to this recommendation, the Research 
and Information System for Developing Countries (RIS) has prepared a Report

budget both through an inter-Ministerial comparison within the Government of 
India and a cross-country comparison with major economies.  
The Committee recommend that MEA should utilize the RIS Report and 
update it annually with the latest figures on both inter-Ministerial allocation 
trends and cross-country comparisons. The updated Report should be

formally annexed to MEA's budget demand submission to the Ministry of

Non-inclusion of Line of Credit Provisioning 
3. The Committee had consistently held that Line of Credit provisioning, 
which represents a notional expenditure and an adjustment of accounts 
between different branches of Government, charged to the Guaranteed 
Redemption Fund, gives a disproportionate and misleading picture of MEA's 
actual expenditure. The Committee are satisfied to note that BE 2026-27 
allocations do not include any provisioning for Lines of Credit (LoC) through 
the EXIM Bank. The Foreign Secretary, during evidence confirmed that the 
Ministry remains engaged with the Reserve Bank of India and the Ministry of 
Finance on this structural issue.  
The Committee reiterate that LoC provisioning must not be included in 
MEA's regular budget in future years. The Committee suggest that this position 
be formalized through a permanent institutional arrangement, whereby such 
provisioning is charged directly to an appropriate dedicated instrument 
managed by the Ministry of Finance and the Reserve Bank of India, entirely 
outside the MEA's Demand for Grants. The Ministry should formally propose 
this structural arrangement to the concerned authorities and report back to the 
Committee on the outcome in the next year.

the MEA’s budgetary demands and the actual allocations. In 2025-26, the

The Committee wish to make it unambiguously clear that the recurring

15. The Committee note that despite the eMigrate portal, the mPassport 
Police App, and the network of PoE offices, illegal recruitment agencies and 
unauthorized intermediaries continue to operate, exploiting vulnerable Indian 
workers seeking employment abroad. The Committee observe that the Ministry 
has acknowledged the challenge of combating fraud in the recruitment 
process and the need for coordination with local police and cyber-crime units,

enforcement actions. The Committee are of the firm view that the protection of 
Indian workers from exploitation, trafficking, and fraudulent recruitment is a 
fundamental obligation of the State, and that the current enforcement 
architecture - characterized by a small PoE network, limited financial 
resources, and dependence on State police coordination - appear insufficient 
to meet this obligation at the required scale.

response mechanism for distress cases involving illegal recruitment. The

faculty members, has MoUs with 103 countries and four plurilateral groupings, 
and has recently launched a Learning Management Software (LMS) platform in 
January 2025 to digitize and modernize its training delivery. 
The Committee are concerned to note that the budgetary allocation for 
SSIFS, which is the sole dedicated training institution for India’s entire foreign 
service cadre, has remained largely unchanged even as the demands of 
modern diplomacy have grown considerably in scope and complexity. With 
India’s diplomatic network expanding to 216 Missions and Posts, and with 

218 | P a g e 
 
diplomats increasingly required to navigate different areas such as geo-
technology, digital diplomacy, international trade negotiations, climate policy, 
and health security alongside traditional foreign policy functions, an annual 
training budget of Rs. 24.37 crore and a permanent faculty strength of 10-12 is, 
in the Committee’s view, clearly inadequate for SSIFS, which is an institution 
of national importance. The Committee also note that the Institute draws 
visiting faculties from retired Indian Ambassadors, reputed domain experts, 
senior officials of MEA and other Ministries.  
The Committee welcome the launch of the LMS platform in January 2025 
and the positive results noted in terms of improved digital proficiency and time 
management among officer trainees. The Committee recommend that the 
budgetary allocation for SSIFS be substantially enhanced in the coming years 
to reflect the growing demands on India’s diplomatic service. The Committee 
are of the view that investment in training India’s diplomats is an investment in 
India’s foreign policy capacity itself, and must be treated as a priority 
expenditure. 
 
Strengthening the Policy Planning and Research Division 
45. The Committee note that the Policy Planning and Research (PP&R) 
Division serves as the nodal Division of the Ministry for medium-term policy 
planning, research, strategic outreach, coordination of India's Neighbourhood 
First Policy, and the Voice of Global South Summit initiative. In addition to 
organising four flagship Track 1.5 initiatives (the Raisina Dialogue, Global 
Technology Summit, Asia Economic Dialogue, and the Indian Ocean 
Conference), the Division also conducts Track 1.0 policy planning dialogues 
with the Foreign Offices of more than 20 countries, manages the Strategic 
Outreach Fund, oversees the MEA Niti Shakti Initiative, coordinates the work of 
ICWA and RIS, and is responsible for the preparation and publication of the 
Ministry's Annual Report. The Committee further note that the Division has 
commendably expanded its outreach beyond New Delhi, with strategic 
dialogues and conferences now being organised across cities such as 
Bengaluru, Mumbai, Kochi, Bhubaneswar, Jaipur, Kolkata, and 

219 | P a g e 
 
Thiruvananthapuram, engaging universities, think tanks, and state 
governments in the foreign policy discourse. 
The Committee are of the view that the PP&R Division carries an 
exceptionally wide and diverse mandate. While the Committee welcome the 
expanding footprint of the Division's activities, it is concerned to note that the 
breadth of administrative, coordination, and event management 
responsibilities placed upon the Division may be drawing attention and 
capacity away from its primary and most critical function, namely substantive 
policy research, strategic analysis, and medium-term foreign policy planning. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry should undertake a 
structured review of the PP&R Division's mandate, activities, and resource 
allocation to ensure that its core intellectual and policy planning functions 
receive the requisite focus and priority. The Committee also urge that the 
Ministry to bring out a brief statement on the key research outputs, policy 
briefs, and strategic assessments produced by the PP&R Division during the 
year, along with an indication of how these have fed into the Ministry's policy 
deliberations and decisions. 
46.  The Committee note that officers posted to the PP&R Division are 
required to track developments across the full spectrum of global affairs,  
geopolitics, geo-economics, and geo-technology  and produce a range of 
outputs including the Daily Report, connecting the dots, Arth Niti, Raksha Niti, 
Tech Niti, Monthly Reports, situation reports, and policy briefs, which are 
disseminated to the Ministry, Missions abroad, and agencies including the 
PMO, Ministry of Defence, and the National Security Council Secretariat. The 
Committee also note that the Ministry has taken positive steps to 
institutionalize external expertise through the MEA Niti Shakti Initiative, which 
enables divisions to commission research from think tanks and universities, 
through the Strategic Outreach Fund. 
The Committee are of the considered view that given the rapidly 
evolving and complex global landscape, the quality and depth of India's 
foreign policy planning is critically dependent on the availability of adequate 
human resources with specialized domain expertise within the PP&R Division, 

220 | P a g e 
 
supplemented by a robust and structured engagement with India's universities 
and think tank community. The Committee are concerned to note that the 
current model of engagement with external institutions, while wide in its reach 
remains largely event-driven and project-specific, and does not appear to be 
anchored in a systematic, long-term framework for knowledge partnership. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Ministry should 
undertake a comprehensive assessment of the human resource requirements 
of the PP&R Division, having regard to the full scope of its mandate, and 
ensure that the Division is adequately staffed with officers with requisite 
domain expertise in specialized areas such as geo-technology, international 
economics, climate diplomacy, and regional studies. The Committee further 
urge the Ministry to move beyond event-based collaboration with think tanks 
and universities towards more enduring, structured knowledge partnerships. 
 
Grand Strategy / Foreign Policy Document 
47. The Committee note that with regard to formulating a grand strategy or a 
comprehensive foreign policy document that clearly articulates India's foreign 
policy objectives, goals, and long-term strategic approach, the Ministry 
submitted that no single overarching and formalised strategic document 
currently exists, and that India's diplomatic principles and priorities are 
expressed through various platforms. The Committee has been furnished with 
a list of 36 countries, including major powers such as the United States, United 
Kingdom, Germany, Japan, and Russia, as well as smaller nations such as 
Estonia, New Zealand, Slovenia, and Bhutan, that have published formal 
foreign policy or national security strategy documents laying out their 
international objectives, priorities, and approaches in a single accessible 
document. 
The Committee are of the considered view that the absence of a formal, 
publicly available foreign policy document is a significant gap for a country of 
India's global stature, ambitions, and expanding international engagement. The 
Ministry's Annual Report, while comprehensive and valuable as a record of the 

221 | P a g e 
 
previous year's diplomatic activities, is inherently a retrospective document. It 
is not a forward-looking strategic document that articulates where India seeks 
to go in the world, what its priorities are, and how it intends to pursue them 
over the medium to long term. The Committee also note that the Ministry has 
acknowledged that there are no obstacles to preparing such a document. In 
this context, the Committee would like to understand why such a document 
has not been prepared thus far, particularly given India's growing global profile 
and its active engagement across bilateral, regional, and multilateral platforms. 
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommend that the Ministry, 
through the PP&R Division, take up on priority the preparation of a formal 
Indian Foreign Policy Document - a publicly available, medium-term strategic 
document that clearly articulates India's foreign policy objectives, regional and 
global priorities, key bilateral and multilateral engagements, and the guiding 
principles of India's approach to the world. The Committee urge the Ministry to 
inform them of the timeline within which this exercise will be completed. 
 
Budgetary allocation to ‘Embassies and Missions’ 
48. The allocation under the sub-head ‘Embassies and Mission’ has been 
progressively enhanced, from Rs. 3,528.85 crore in BE 2023-24 to Rs. 4,206.22 
crore in BE 2025-26 and Rs. 5,059.30 crore in BE 2026-27, reflecting the 
growing scale and complexity of India’s diplomatic engagements. The 
Committee observe that the RE stage has consistently seen significant 
augmentation. In 2025-26, the RE allocation of Rs. 4,632.27 crore, which was 
Rs. 426.05 crore above the BE. The Committee note with concern that in each 
of the past four years, actual expenditure has broadly been in line with the RE 
allocations, underlining that the BE stage consistently underestimates the 
Ministry’s genuine resource requirements for its Missions abroad. 
The Ministry has explained that the enhanced BE 2026-27 allocation 
includes provisioning for five new Missions and Posts operationalized in 2026-
27 and that the Ministry starts ‘from a lower base’ at BE with augmentation 
sought at RE. The Committee are of the view that this may lead to mid-year 
disruptions in Mission’s functioning and uncertainty in fiscal planning. The 

222 | P a g e 
 
Committee strongly recommend that the Ministry should move away from the 
practice of under-provisioning for the ‘Embassies and Missions’ head at BE 
stage and routinely seeking correction at RE. The practice of beginning ‘from a 
lower base’ may distort the budgetary picture, weakens the Ministry’s case 
before the Ministry of Finance, and create operational uncertainty for 
Missions/Posts. The Committee also recommend that the Ministry should also 
develop and maintain a consolidated database of per-Mission expenditure 
across all heads, updated on a quarterly basis, to enable more precise 
budgetary planning. 
 
Geographical Spread of Embassies and Posts abroad 
49. The Committee note that India currently maintains 219 Missions and 
Posts across the world, making it one of the most expansive diplomatic 
networks among developing nations. In the last financial year, one new 
Mission in Quito (Ecuador) and four new Posts in Boston (USA), Los Angeles 
(USA), Kazan (Russia) and Yekaterinburg (Russia) have been operationalized. 
The Committee welcome India’s expanding diplomatic footprint and note that 
this expansion has been driven by a considered assessment of bilateral 
potential, trade and investment priorities, diaspora presence, and India’s 
growing multilateral leadership.  
The Committee note, however, that as of date, India does not have 
resident Missions in 40 UN member countries. While many of these are small 
island states where concurrent accreditation may be sufficient, the list also 
includes countries of diplomatic and strategic significance such as Andorra, 
Bosnia and Herzegovina, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Montenegro, 
North Macedonia, Moldova, Nicaragua, and Uruguay. The Ministry has 
acknowledged that the scope and depth of bilateral relations with countries 
lacking resident Indian Missions is regularly reviewed. The Committee are of 
the view that this review must be formalized and its outcomes made more 
transparent. The Ministry should carry out a comprehensive assessment of the 
40 countries where India lacks resident Missions, identifying priority cases and 
roadmap for early Mission establishment.

Security of Indian Missions and Posts Abroad 
50. The Committee note with concern that the Ministry does not have a 
dedicated budget head for the security of Indian Missions and Posts abroad, 
and that security expenditure is met from establishment heads “as per 
requirement.” The Committee are of the view that this arrangement may be 
fundamentally inadequate in a period of heightened geopolitical tensions, 
multiple active conflict zones, and increased targeting of diplomatic premises 
globally. The Committee note that the funding of expenditure for security of 
Indian diplomats, mission staff, and consular facilities from general 
establishment heads may not be adequate to address the systematic threat 
environment that Indian Missions face. The Committee strongly recommend 
that the Ministry create a dedicated budget sub-head for Mission Security, with 
a specific annual allocation based on a comprehensive threat assessment and 
security audit of all Indian Missions and Posts abroad. The Committee further 
recommend that the Ministry should conduct an immediate comprehensive 
security audit of all Indian Missions, prioritizing high-risk locations including 
conflict zones, countries with strained bilateral relations, and locations with 
known security vulnerabilities, along with a time-bound security enhancement 
plan and its budgetary implications. 
 
Monitoring Mechanism for Embassies and Posts abroad 
51. Recognizing the importance of an effective monitoring mechanism for 
ensuring the optimal performance of Indian Missions and Posts abroad, the 
Committee note the establishment of the Performance Evaluation and 
Monitoring System (PEMS) by the Ministry in 2016. The Ministry is currently 
evaluating the performance of 203 Missions/Posts for FY 2024-25 under PEMS 
6.0. The Committee note that PEMS evaluation scores feed into a physical 
inspection cycle conducted by the Directorate General of Inspections (DGI), 
with inspection findings followed up through Action Taken Reports until 
compliance is achieved. The Committee also note the Ministry’s deployment of 
multiple technology platforms for Mission operations, including IMAS 2.0 for 
integrated mission accounting, MEADOWS for HR management, the MADAD 

224 | P a g e 
 
portal for consular grievance redressal, eMigrate for emigration processing, 
and the 3Ts (Trade, Tourism and Technology) dashboard for economic 
diplomacy tracking.  
Acknowledging the efforts of the Ministry towards making the PEMS 
interface more user friendly, the Committee recommend that periodic feedback 
surveys from the Missions and Posts should be regularly conducted to identify 
scope for further improvements. The Committee desire to be apprised of the 
current status of the performance evaluation being done for the 203 
Missions/Posts abroad under PMS 6.0 and therefore Ministry may furnish a 
report on the performance of India’s Mission network, drawing on PEMS data 
and DGI inspection findings in its Action Taken Replies.  
 
Human capital at Mission and Posts abroad 
52. The Committee note that as of 1 January 2026, the sanctioned strength 
of the Ministry stands at 6,035, of which 54.08% are located in Missions and 
Posts abroad, with an additional local cadre strength of 3,179 at 
Missions/Posts. The Ministry has stated that vacancies are regularly reviewed 
and officers posted against vacancies. However, the Committee observe that 
the Ministry has not provided the Committee with the vacancy position, that is, 
how many of the 6,035 sanctioned posts are actually filled, which cadres have 
the highest vacancy rates, and what is the Ministry’s specific recruitment and 
filling timeline. The Committee recommend that the Ministry should furnish a 
complete cadre-wise statement of sanctioned strength, filled positions, 
vacancies and expected timeline for filling vacancies for each cadre within the 
Ministry, both at Headquarters and at Missions/Posts abroad. 
 
Nalanda University 
53. The Committee acknowledge the steadfast commitment of the 
Government of India in reviving the ancient seat of learning through Nalanda 
University, established under the Nalanda University Act, 2010 as an

international institution under the East Asia Summit (EAS) framework with 17 
member countries as founding partners. The Committee note with satisfaction 
that a state-of-the-art Net-Zero sustainable campus spanning approximately 
455 acres was formally inaugurated by the Prime Minister in June 2024. 
Notwithstanding this milestone, the Committee observe that construction of 
the Central Library and the 2,000-seater auditorium remain to be completed. 
The Committee also note that the project faced significant time and cost 
overruns on account of the remote location of the campus, the logistical 
challenges of mobilizing skilled manpower, and the severe disruptions caused 
by the COVID-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2022. 
The Committee express their concern that despite its founding premise 
as a collectively supported international institution, financial contributions 
from EAS member countries have been both minimal and largely confined to 
the University’s early years. Twelve of the seventeen founding partner 
countries have made no contribution. The burden of sustaining the University 
has fallen almost entirely on the Government of India. The Committee welcome 
the constitution of an Endowment Committee to develop a fundraising strategy 
covering philanthropic donations, corporate sponsorships, and support from 
global foundations. 
The Committee reiterate their concern, expressed in previous reports, 
that the financial engagement of EAS founding partner countries with Nalanda 
University has remained inadequate. The Committee recommend that the 
Ministry should move beyond general diplomatic encouragement and design a 
structured, time-bound initiative to secure meaningful financial commitments 
from EAS member countries, with specific bilateral engagement at an 
appropriately senior level. The Committee would like to be apprised of the 
outcome of these efforts.  
54. The Committee note that Nalanda University has made significant 
academic progress since commencing operations in 2014. The University now 
operates six Schools: Historical Studies, Ecology and Environment Studies, 
Buddhist Studies, Philosophy and Comparative Religions, Languages and 
Literature, Management Studies, and International Relations and Peace

Studies, and offers over 30 academic programmes. Total student enrolment 
stands at 1,925 in 2025-26 from an initial intake of 12 students in 2014-15. The 
Committee further note that Nalanda University is the nodal institution of the 
ASEAN-India University Network (AINU) and has established bilateral MoUs 
with institutions across Asia, Europe, and North America, including partners in 
Japan, Republic of Korea, Indonesia, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, Nepal, 
Mongolia, Russia, Spain, the United States, and the Czech Republic. The 
Committee were informed by MEA that AINU-related collaborations are fully 
funded by the ASEAN Secretariat, ensuring that they do not place a financial 
burden on the University. The Committee, however, note that these 
collaborations, while wide in geographical reach, have yet to translate into a 
globally recognized research output or academic reputation. 
In the considered opinion of the Committee, with the substantial 
operationalization of the permanent campus, the University must transition 
decisively from a phase of infrastructure development to one of academic 
consolidation and excellence. The Committee reiterate that the University’s 
long-term credibility as an instrument of India’s educational diplomacy will 
depend on the quality and global standing of its academic and research 
output. The Committee recommend that the Ministry, in consultation with 
Nalanda University’s Governing Board, should prepare an academic 
development plan covering projected enrolment targets for each programme 
stream, proposed new academic offerings, faculty recruitment timelines, and 
research output goals.

55. In spite of its regional significance as a flagship initiative under SAARC, 
the tardy progress in the establishment and operationalization of the South 
Asian University remains a matter of concern to the Committee. The 
Committee note that the capital budget of SAU is sourced entirely from India, 
with the Union Cabinet in 2009 approving a contribution of USD 198 million 
towards capital expenditure, of which USD 171.461 million has been disbursed 
to date. Construction of the permanent campus has been undertaken in 

227 | P a g e 
 
packages: Package I (boundary wall) and Package II (five buildings) are 
complete; Package III (seven buildings, including the Library, Convention 
Centre, and Administration building) is 98% complete; and the scope of 
Package IV is under consideration. The Committee note that the capital works 
have been significantly delayed on account of Gram Sabha land issues, forest 
land encumbrances, geo-morphological complications, the COVID-19 
pandemic, and frequent construction bans imposed by the National Green 
Tribunal. 
The Committee note that SAU’s operational budget is contributed by all 
eight SAARC member states, with India’s share standing at 59.8%. The 
Committee reiterate their concern, expressed in successive reports, that 
several SAARC member states continue to default on their operational budget 
contributions. The Ministry has itself acknowledged that these pending dues 
affect day-to-day operations, constrain SAU’s ability to project itself as a well-
managed institution, and limit its academic collaborations with global partners. 
The Committee are disheartened to note that despite repeated follow-ups at 
SAU Governing Board meetings and SAARC Programming Committee 
meetings, the problem of default payments by member state has remained 
unresolved year after year. 
The Committee reiterate their concern that India bears 100% of the 
capital cost and 59.8% of the operational cost of SAU, a burden wholly 
inconsistent with the foundational premise of the University as a collectively 
owned and jointly managed regional institution. The Committee strongly 
recommend that the Government of India should take up the matter of pending 
dues with defaulting member states at the highest diplomatic level, going well 
beyond Governing Board and SAARC Programming Committee meetings, and 
engaging through bilateral channels at an appropriate senior level. The 
Committee further urge that Package III be completed without any further 
delay, that the scope and timeline for Package IV be finalized, and that a 
revised cost statement against the approved USD 198 million outlay be 
furnished.

56. The Committee note that South Asian University has made tangible 
academic progress since its establishment, growing from an initial intake of 50 
students in 2010-11 to a current intake of 1,105 in 2025-26, with total enrolment 
standing at 1,756. The University now offers 5 Bachelor’s, 12 Master’s, and 9 
Ph.D. programmes across disciplines including Computer Science, 
Economics, Biotechnology, International Relations, Sociology, Law, and 
Business Administration. The University has set an ambitious target of 4,000 
students by 2029-30. 
While welcoming this trajectory, the Committee, are concerned to note 
that this expansion in student numbers is occurring against a backdrop of 
chronic financial stress caused by member state defaults, which constrains 
faculty recruitment, scholarship offerings, and academic collaborations with 
global institutions. The Committee recommend that the Ministry should ensure 
that SAU’s expansion towards the 4,000-student target is matched by 
commensurate growth in faculty strength, academic infrastructure, residential 
capacity, and financial resources. A university that is growing rapidly in 
student numbers while facing operational funding uncertainty is particularly 
vulnerable to deterioration in the quality of its academic offering, which would 
defeat the very purpose for which SAU was established. The Committee 
recommend that the Ministry should identify and pursue specific steps, within 
the existing governance framework, to strengthen SAU’s academic profile and 
international visibility, including by facilitating research partnerships with 
Indian universities and research institutions, extending SAARC Silver Jubilee 
Scholarships to a wider cohort of students, and supporting SAU’s participation 
in regional academic networks and knowledge-exchange platforms. SAU’s 
potential as a symbol of India’s commitment to regional integration and as a 
platform for people-to-people connectivity within South Asia can only be 
realized if the institution is demonstrably well-resourced, well-managed, and 
academically credible.

Assistance to autonomous bodies and institutions 
57. The Committee note that the Ministry of External Affairs provides 
Grants-in-Aid to autonomous bodies and institutions, principally the Indian 
Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR), the Indian Council of World Affairs 
(ICWA), and the Research and Information System for Developing Countries 
(RIS).  These institutions are not administrative extensions of the Ministry but 
are the intellectual and cultural infrastructure through which India’s diplomacy 
acquires depth, reach, and the capacity to engage the world beyond the formal.

Ministry has put in place an established accountability framework for these 
institutions.  
The Committee observe that while the budgetary allocation for this head 
has grown incrementally, the Committee are of the view that the increase is 
modest relative to the scale of India’s foreign policy objectives. Further, there 
is a lack of structured and outcome-oriented framework that links the research 
mandates of these institutions to the Ministry’s identified foreign policy 
priorities. The Committee urge the Ministry to establish a formal, structured 
mechanism for integrating the research outputs of ICWA and RIS into MEA’s 
foreign policy formulation process. The Committee further recommend that the 
Ministry, in coordination with ICCR, ICWA, and RIS, should develop a 
coordinated global outreach strategy that identifies countries of priority 
strategic importance, where the combined intellectual and cultural presence of

unfunded gap of Rs. 18.71 crore at the Revised Estimates stage of 2026-27 so
